a least-squares solution of $Ax=b$, and among all least-squares solutions it

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$. **Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then Lebesgue outer measure $\lambda_n^*$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]) is an outer measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-outer-measure]]): it vanishes at $\varnothing$, is monotone, and is
countably subadditive.

**The agreement clause is a theorem of ZF and needs no choice principle:**
$\lambda_n^*(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every elementary set $A$
([[def-elementary-set-in-rn]]), where $\mu_0$ is elementary volume. In
particular $\lambda_n^*(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
and $\lambda_n^*(\varnothing) = 0$.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. **Degenerate boxes.** If $a_i \le b_i$ are reals with $a_{i_0} = b_{i_0}$ for
   some $i_0 < n$, then every set $R$ between the open box
   $\{x : a_i < x_i < b_i\ (i<n)\}$ and the closed rectangle $[a,b]$ is Lebesgue
   measurable with $\lambda_n(R) = 0$.
2. **Coordinate hyperplanes.** For $i_0 < n$ and a real $c$, the set
   $$H_{i_0,c} \;:=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x_{i_0} = c \,\}$$
   is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(H_{i_0,c}) = 0$.

At $n = 1$ the hyperplane $H_{0,c}$ is the singleton $\{c\}$.

derivations.claim: For $n$ large enough that $t_n:=(n/(2\log n))^{1/d}\ge2$, put $m_n=\lfloor t_n\rfloor$ and partition each coordinate interval of $\Omega$ into $m_n$ equal half-open intervals, closing the last interval at its right endpoint. This gives $m_n^d$ disjoint cells covering $\Omega$. Each cell differs from a half-open box with the same coordinate bounds only on its boundary faces, which lie in finitely many coordinate hyperplanes. By [F4] those hyperplanes and every subset of their union are measurable and null, so each cell is measurable and has the same measure as that half-open box, namely $(L/m_n)^d$ by [F1]. The same argument for the boundary of $\Omega$ gives $\lambda_d(\Omega)=L^d$. Hence normalized Lebesgue measure assigns each cell probability $(L/m_n)^d/L^d=m_n^{-d}$.

For a fixed cell, independence [F3] gives probability $(1-m_n^{-d})^n\le e^{-n/m_n^d}$ that it is empty. By [F2], the probability that some cell is empty is at most $m_n^d e^{-n/m_n^d}\le n e^{-2\log n}=1/n$, because $m_n^d\le n/(2\log n)$ and hence $n/m_n^d\ge2\log n$.

On the complementary event every cell contains a sample point. Every $x\in\Omega$ belongs to one cell, whose Euclidean diameter is $L\sqrt d/m_n$; therefore $h_n\le L\sqrt d/m_n$. Since $t_n\ge2$ implies $m_n=\lfloor t_n\rfloor\ge t_n/2$, we obtain $$h_n\le2L\sqrt d\left(\frac{2\log n}{n}\right)^{1/d} =C_dL\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{1/d}.$$ The event has probability at least $1-1/n$ by step 2.1.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\xi_{ij})_{i,j\ge1}$ be one infinite iid array of real random variables with mean zero, variance one and finite fourth moment. For each $n$, let $p_n$ be a positive integer with $p_n/n\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)\setminus\{1\}$ and let $X_n=(\xi_{ij})_{1\le i\le n,\,1\le j\le p_n}$ be the upper-left block. Let $\beta_n\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$ be deterministic with $\|\beta_n\|_2=r>0$. Let $\varepsilon_n\in\mathbb R^n$ have independent centered components of variance $\sigma^2$, independent of $X_n$ (so its covariance is $\sigma^2I_n$), and let $z_{0,n}\in\mathbb R^{p_n}$ be independent of $(X_n,\varepsilon_n)$ with mean zero and covariance  $I_{p_n}$. Set $y_n=X_n\beta_n+\varepsilon_n$, $\widehat\beta_n=X_n^+y_n$, and $S_n=X_n^{\mathsf T}X_n/n$. Define the design-conditional prediction risk by $\mathcal R_n=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon_n,z_{0,n}}[(z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}\widehat\beta_n-z_{0,n}^{\mathsf T}\beta_n)^2\mid X_n]$. If $\gamma<1$, then almost surely $\mathcal R_n\to\sigma^2\gamma/(1-\gamma)$. If $\gamma>1$, then almost surely $\mathcal R_n\to r^2(1-1/\gamma)+\sigma^2/(\gamma-1)$.

Let $n,p\ge1$, let $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R^p$
be deterministic, and let $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R^n$ and
$z_0\in\mathbb R^p$ be independent of one another and of $X$, with
$\mathbb E\varepsilon=0$, $\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon)=\sigma^2I_n$,
$\mathbb Ez_0=0$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(z_0)=I_p$. Set
$y=X\beta+\varepsilon$, $\widehat\beta=X^+y$,
$S=X^{\mathsf T}X/n$, and
$$\mathcal R(X):=\mathbb E_{\varepsilon,z_0} \left[(z_0^{\mathsf T}(\widehat\beta-\beta))^2\mid X\right].$$
Then
$$\mathcal R(X)=\|(I_p-X^+X)\beta\|_2^2+ \sigma^2\operatorname{tr}((X^{\mathsf T}X)^+) =\|(I_p-X^+X)\beta\|_2^2+ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\operatorname{tr}(S^+).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $p\ge1$ and $\sigma>0$, the Gaussian radial kernel on $\mathbb R^p$ is $k_\sigma(x,z)=\exp(-\|x-z\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))$. It is a real positive semidefinite kernel, including on finite samples with repeated points or a singular Gram matrix.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every set $X$ and every real positive semidefinite kernel $k$ on $X$, the canonical construction from finitely supported coefficients, quotient by zero seminorm, and norm completion defines a real reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal H_k$. For every $x\in X$, its kernel section $k_x=k(\cdot,x)$ belongs to $\mathcal H_k$ and satisfies $\langle h,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H_k}=h(x)$ for all $h\in\mathcal H_k$. The choice assumption here is countable choice; this statement does not assert the same construction in ZF without that assumption.

A **real kernel** on a set $X$ is a function $k:X\times X\to\mathbb R$. It is **positive semidefinite** if it is symmetric and, for every integer $n\ge1$, every $x_1,\ldots,x_n\in X$, and every $c_1,\ldots,c_n\in\mathbb R$,

$$\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i,x_j)\ge0.$$

A **real reproducing kernel Hilbert space with kernel $k$** is a real Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ of functions $X\to\mathbb R$ such that, for each $x\in X$, the section $k_x:=k(\cdot,x)$ lies in $\mathcal H$ and $\langle f,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=f(x)$ for every $f\in\mathcal H$. Consequently $\langle k_z,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H}=k(z,x)=k(x,z)$.

For the canonical construction, let $E_0$ be the real vector space of finitely supported functions $a:X\to\mathbb R$, write $\delta_x$ for the function supported at $x$ with value $1$, and put

$$B(a,b):=\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}\sum_{z\in\operatorname{supp}(b)}a(x)b(z)k(x,z).$$

Let $N:=\{a\in E_0:B(a,a)=0\}$. The canonical space is formed by giving $E_0/N$ its induced inner product and taking a norm completion; the image of $\delta_x$ is denoted $k_x$. For an element $h$ of that completion, its associated function is $x\mapsto\langle h,k_x\rangle$. The quotient, completed inner product, and function identification are justified by the local construction theorem.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a fixed closed cube with
positive side length, let $\sigma>0$, and set
$k_\sigma(x,z)=\exp(-\|x-z\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))$ on $\Omega$. Let
$\mathcal H_\sigma$ be its real reproducing-kernel Hilbert space. For a finite
nonempty set $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subset\Omega$, define its Euclidean fill
distance and Gaussian power function by
$$h_X:=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{1\le j\le m}\|x-x_j\|_2,\qquad P_X(x):=\inf_{v\in\operatorname{span}\{k_\sigma(\cdot,x_j):1\le j\le m\}} \|k_\sigma(\cdot,x)-v\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}.$$
There are constants $C,c,h_0>0$, depending only on $d,\Omega,\sigma$, such
that every such $X$ with $0<h_X\le h_0$ satisfies
$$\sup_{x\in\Omega}P_X(x)\le C\exp\!\left(-c\frac{|\log h_X|}{h_X}\right).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let
$\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_j,a_j+L]$ be a closed cube with
$L>0$, and let $U_1,U_2,\ldots$ be independent random vectors, each distributed
according to normalized Lebesgue measure on $\Omega$. For $n\ge1$, define the
Euclidean fill distance

$$h_n:=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{1\le i\le n}\|x-U_i\|_2.$$

There are constants $C_d=2\sqrt d\,2^{1/d}$ and $n_d$ such that, for every
$n\ge n_d$,

$$\mathbb P\!\left\{h_n\le C_dL\left(\frac{\log n}{n}\right)^{1/d}\right\} \ge1-\frac1n.$$

Let $E$ be a real inner-product space, let $M\subseteq E$ be a finite-dimensional subspace, and let $f\in E$. There is a unique $p\in M$ such that $f-p$ is orthogonal to every vector of $M$. This vector is the unique nearest point in $M$ to $f$, and it satisfies $\|p\|\le\|f\|$. The conclusion does not require $E$ to be complete.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Then $g(x_i)=0$, so [F3] gives $\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x_i)\rangle=0$ for each $i$ and hence $g\perp V_n$. By [F6] the projection $\Pi_{V_n}$ exists; therefore $$g(x)=\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x)\rangle =\langle g,k_\sigma(\cdot,x)-\Pi_{V_n}k_\sigma(\cdot,x)\rangle.$$ The inner-product Cauchy--Schwarz inequality follows by expanding $\|u-tv\|^2\ge0$ and minimizing over real $t$ (with the zero-vector case immediate). Thus $|g(x)|\le\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}P_{X_n}(x)$.

The triangle inequality gives $\|g\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}\le\|h\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}+\|h^*\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}$. Taking the supremum in step 1.1 yields $$\sup_{x\in\Omega}|h(x)-h^*(x)|\le (\|h\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}+\|h^*\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}) \sup_{x\in\Omega}P_{X_n}(x).$$

Write $\Omega=v+Q[0,L]^d$ using its side length $L>0$ and an orthogonal matrix $Q$, and put $u_i=Q^{\mathsf T}(x_i-v)$. The affine map $F(u)=v+Qu$ bijects the product cube $C_0=[0,L]^d$ onto $\Omega$. For every Borel $E\subseteq C_0$, [F7] gives $\mathbb P(u_i\in E)=\lambda_d(F(E))/\lambda_d(\Omega)=|\det Q|\lambda_d(E)/(|\det Q|\lambda_d(C_0))=\lambda_d(E)/\lambda_d(C_0)$. The transformed samples remain independent: for finitely many Borel sets $E_i\subseteq C_0$, their joint event is $\bigcap_i\{x_i\in F(E_i)\}$, and independence of the $x_i$ makes its probability the product of the individual probabilities. These events are measurable since $F$ is a homeomorphism. Also $\|F(u)-F(w)\|_2=\|u-w\|_2$, so the fill distance of $\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}$ in $C_0$ equals $h_{X_n}$ in $\Omega$. By [F5], on an event of probability at least $1-1/n$, the fill distance $h_{X_n}$ is at most $\bar h_n=C_dL(\log n/n)^{1/d}$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $\bar h_n<\min(h_0,e^{-1})$; the function $u\mapsto|\log u|/u$ is decreasing on $(0,e^{-1}]$, so [F4] applies and gives $$\sup_xP_{X_n}(x)\le C\exp\!\left(-c\frac{|\log h_{X_n}|}{h_{X_n}}\right) \le C\exp\!\left(-\frac{c}{\bar h_n}\right) =C\exp\!\left(-\frac{c}{C_dL}\left(\frac{n}{\log n}\right)^{1/d}\right).$$ Using this bound in step 2.1 proves the displayed estimate with $A=C$ and $B=c/(C_dL)$, uniformly for every interpolant on that event.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

derivations.claim: We first prove that for every real univariate polynomial $r$ of degree at most $N\ge1$, $$|r'(u)|\le\frac{100N}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\sup_{-1\le v\le1}|r(v)|\qquad(-1<u<1).$$ For $m\ge1$ define the finite trigonometric polynomial $$F_m(t)=\sum_{|k|<m}(1-|k|/m)e^{ikt}=\frac1m\left|\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}e^{ijt}\right|^2=\frac{\sin^2(mt/2)}{m\sin^2(t/2)}.$$ Here $i^2=-1$; the square identity follows by expanding the finite sum and counting pairs of indices with a prescribed difference, and the last identity follows from the finite geometric series, with continuous values at multiples of $2\pi$. For $|t|\le1/m$, differentiate the finite Fourier sum to obtain $|F'_m(t)|\le\sum_{|k|<m}|k|(1-|k|/m)\le m^2$. For $1/m\le|t|\le\pi$, differentiating the sine quotient gives $$|F'_m(t)|\le\frac{\pi^2}{t^2}+\frac{\pi^3}{m|t|^3},$$ because $|\sin(t/2)|\ge|t|/\pi$. This sine bound follows on $[0,\pi/2]$ by concavity of sine, whose second derivative is $-\sin\le0$, applied to the chord joining $(0,0)$ and $(\pi/2,1)$; symmetry gives the negative arguments.

Put $Q=[-1,1]^d$ and $Q_c=[-1/2,1/2]^d$. For a univariate polynomial of degree at most $n$, interpolate at $t_j=-1/2+j/n$ for $0\le j\le n$. The interpolation identity holds because its difference from the polynomial has degree at most $n$ and $n+1$ distinct roots; the root bound follows by successively factoring each distinct root. For $|t|\le1$ the absolute value of the $j$th Lagrange polynomial is at most $(3/2)^n n^n/(j!(n-j)!)$: numerator factors are at most $3/2$ and its denominator has absolute value $n^{-n}j!(n-j)!$. Summing these bounds gives $(3n)^n/n!\le(3e)^n$, where $$\log(n!)=\sum_{j=1}^n\log j\ge\int_1^n\log t\,dt=n\log n-n+1$$ proves $n!\ge(n/e)^n$. Applying this univariate estimate in each coordinate in turn, and taking suprema after each application, shows for every polynomial $p$ of total degree at most $n$ that $$\|p\|_Q\le R^n\|p\|_{Q_c},\qquad R=(3e)^d,$$ since its degree in each separate coordinate is at most $n$. Here and below $\|p\|_E=\sup_{z\in E}|p(z)|$.

Integrating the bounds of step 1.1 over $[-\pi,\pi]$, with the near-zero interval contributing at most $2m$ and the other terms bounded by extending their elementary integrals to infinity, gives $$\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|F'_m(t)|\,dt\le\frac{2+2\pi^2+\pi^3}{2\pi}m\le20m.$$ For $m=1$ this also holds because $F_1=1$. Define $V_N=2F_{2N}-F_N$. Its Fourier coefficients for every $|k|\le N$ equal $1$: for $|k|<N$ they are $2(1-|k|/(2N))-(1-|k|/N)$, and for $|k|=N$ they are $2(1/2)$. For any trigonometric polynomial $T$ of degree at most $N$, integration of finite sums, using $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{ikt}\,dt=0$ for nonzero integer $k$ and $2\pi$ for $k=0$, therefore gives $$T(t)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}T(s)V_N(t-s)\,ds.$$ Differentiating this finite-sum identity and using periodicity and the integral bound yields $\|T'\|_\infty\le100N\|T\|_\infty$. Taking $T(t)=r(\cos t)$, a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $N$ by expansion of powers of cosine, and using $T'(t)=-\sin(t)r'(\cos t)$ proves the inequality announced in step 1.1. All integrals here integrate continuous finite trigonometric sums or the displayed elementary bounds.

Define constants depending only on $d$ by $$a=(3/4)^d,\quad\delta=\min\{1/4,a/(8R)\},\quad G=600\sqrt d/\sqrt\delta,\quad\kappa=\min\{\delta/2,1/(2G)\},\quad A=2R/a.$$ Let $Y\subset Q$ be finite and nonempty with Euclidean fill distance $\eta$ and $n\eta\le\kappa$. The zero polynomial satisfies the desired inequality, so fix nonzero $p$ of degree at most $n$ and set $$q(u)=p(u)\prod_{i=1}^d(1-u_i^2)^n,\qquad S=\|q\|_Q,\qquad M=\max_{y\in Y}|p(y)|.$$ The coordinate degrees of $q$ are at most $3n$. On $Q_c$ its product weight is at least $a^n$, so $S\ge a^n\|p\|_{Q_c}>0$. The last inequality holds because a polynomial vanishing on a box with nonempty interior vanishes identically: fix all but one coordinate in the interior and apply the univariate root bound, then repeat in each coordinate. If some $|u_i|\ge1-\delta$, then $1-u_i^2\le2\delta$ while all other weight factors are at most $1$, and step 1.2 implies $$|q(u)|\le(2\delta)^n\|p\|_Q\le(2\delta R)^n\|p\|_{Q_c}\le(1/4)^nS<S.$$ The maximum of $|q|$ is attained on $Q$ by compactness and the extreme value theorem, so a maximizer $u_*$ lies in $[-1+\delta,1-\delta]^d$.

Take $y\in Y$ with $\|y-u_*\|_2\le\eta$; such a point exists because the minimum over the finite set is attained and is at most its supremum $\eta$. Since $\eta\le\kappa\le\delta/2$, the segment from $u_*$ to $y$ lies where every coordinate has absolute value at most $1-\delta/2$. Apply step 2.1 to each univariate coordinate slice of $q$, of degree at most $3n$ and norm at most $S$ on $[-1,1]$. At each point of this segment it gives $$|\partial_iq|\le\frac{300nS}{\sqrt{\delta-\delta^2/4}}\le\frac{600nS}{\sqrt\delta},\qquad\|\nabla q\|_2\le GnS.$$ Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to the univariate polynomial $t\mapsto q(u_*+t(y-u_*))$: it follows directly here by integrating each power in this finite polynomial. With the Euclidean Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, obtained by expanding $\sum_i(v_i-sw_i)^2\ge0$ and minimizing the quadratic in $s$, this gives $$S\le|q(y)|+Gn\eta S\le M+S/2.$$ Thus $S\le2M$, and steps 1.2 and 2.2 yield $$\|p\|_Q\le R^n\|p\|_{Q_c}\le(R/a)^nS\le2(R/a)^nM\le A^nM.$$ This also includes the zero polynomial.

Fix $x\in Q$, enumerate $Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_m\}$, and let $v(u)\in\mathbb R^D$ be the vector of all monomials in $u$ of total degree at most $n$, in any fixed order, where $D$ is their finite number. Let $K$ be the convex hull of $\{v(y_j),-v(y_j):1\le j\le m\}$. More explicitly it is the image of the closed bounded simplex of $2m$ nonnegative real coordinates summing to $1$, under the continuous map taking these coordinates to the corresponding weighted sum of these $2m$ vectors. Thus $K$ is nonempty and compact, and is convex because convex combinations of two sets of simplex weights remain simplex weights. Suppose $v(x)\notin A^nK$. The continuous squared distance from $v(x)$ attains a minimum at some $z\in A^nK$; put $b=v(x)-z\ne0$. For each $w\in A^nK$ the segment $z+t(w-z)$, $0\le t\le1$, lies in $A^nK$. Its squared distance to $v(x)$ equals $$\|b\|_2^2-2t\,b\mathbin\cdot(w-z)+t^2\|w-z\|_2^2.$$ Minimality at $t=0$ forces $b\mathbin\cdot(w-z)\le0$, since a strictly positive value would make this displayed expression smaller for sufficiently small positive $t$.

Therefore $b\mathbin\cdot z$ is the maximum of the linear functional $b\mathbin\cdot w$ on $A^nK$. A linear functional on this convex hull has maximum equal to the largest of its values on its finite generators: every convex weighted average is at most that largest value and that value is attained at a generator. Consequently $$b\mathbin\cdot v(x)=b\mathbin\cdot z+\|b\|_2^2>A^n\max_{1\le j\le m}|b\mathbin\cdot v(y_j)|.$$ This contradicts step 3.1 applied to the polynomial $u\mapsto b\mathbin\cdot v(u)$, because $x\in Q$. Thus $v(x)\in A^nK$. Write it as $A^n$ times a convex combination of the vectors $\pm v(y_j)$, with nonnegative weights $t_j^+,t_j^-$ summing to $1$. For $\lambda_j=A^n(t_j^+-t_j^-)$ one has $$v(x)=\sum_j\lambda_jv(y_j),\qquad\sum_j|\lambda_j|\le A^n\sum_j(t_j^++t_j^-)=A^n.$$ Taking the scalar product with the coefficient vector of any polynomial of degree at most $n$ proves simultaneous reproduction. This argument uses finite-dimensional compactness and a single minimum, without an infinite choice principle.

Finally choose orthonormal coordinates along the edges of $\Omega$, with its center as origin, and multiply these coordinates by $2/L$. This affine map carries $\Omega$ to $Q$ and scales Euclidean distances by $2/L$, so it carries $X$ to a set $Y$ of fill distance $\eta=2h_X/L$. Composition in either direction preserves total polynomial degree because each coordinate is affine linear. The condition in the Statement is exactly $n\eta\le\kappa$. Transporting the norming inequality from step 3.1 and the coefficients from step 5.1 proves both assertions on $\Omega$, including rotated cubes. All selections made in the proof are finite or individual existential choices, so no choice axiom is used.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $p\ge1$ and $\sigma>0$, the Gaussian radial kernel on $\mathbb R^p$ is $k_\sigma(x,z)=\exp(-\|x-z\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))$. It is a real positive semidefinite kernel, including on finite samples with repeated points or a singular Gram matrix.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every set $X$ and every real positive semidefinite kernel $k$ on $X$, the canonical construction from finitely supported coefficients, quotient by zero seminorm, and norm completion defines a real reproducing kernel Hilbert space $\mathcal H_k$. For every $x\in X$, its kernel section $k_x=k(\cdot,x)$ belongs to $\mathcal H_k$ and satisfies $\langle h,k_x\rangle_{\mathcal H_k}=h(x)$ for all $h\in\mathcal H_k$. The choice assumption here is countable choice; this statement does not assert the same construction in ZF without that assumption.

Let $E$ be a real inner-product space, let $M\subseteq E$ be a finite-dimensional subspace, and let $f\in E$. There is a unique $p\in M$ such that $f-p$ is orthogonal to every vector of $M$. This vector is the unique nearest point in $M$ to $f$, and it satisfies $\|p\|\le\|f\|$. The conclusion does not require $E$ to be complete.

For each integer $d\ge1$ there are constants $A>1$ and $\kappa>0$ with the following property. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be any closed cube of positive side length $L$, including a rotated cube, and let $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subset\Omega$ be finite and nonempty. Define its Euclidean fill distance by
$$h_X=\sup_{z\in\Omega}\min_{1\le j\le m}\|z-x_j\|_2.$$
For every integer $n\ge1$ with $2nh_X/L\le\kappa$, every real polynomial $p$ of total degree at most $n$ satisfies
$$\sup_{z\in\Omega}|p(z)|\le A^n\max_{1\le j\le m}|p(x_j)|.$$
Moreover, for each $x\in\Omega$ there exist real coefficients $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m$, independent of $p$, such that simultaneously for all such polynomials
$$p(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_jp(x_j),\qquad \sum_{j=1}^m|\lambda_j|\le A^n.$$
No separation or Cartesian arrangement of the points is assumed. No choice principle is required.

derivations.claim: Let $z_c$ be the center of $\Omega$, let $L>0$ be its side length, and use orthonormal coordinates along its edges, writing $u(z)$ for the coordinates of $z-z_c$. These coordinates preserve distances and give $\|u(z)\|_2\le B=L\sqrt d/2$ for every $z\in\Omega$. Put $t=B^2/\sigma^2>0$. For a multi-index $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)\in\mathbb N_0^d$, write $|\alpha|=\sum_i\alpha_i$, $\alpha!=\prod_i\alpha_i!$, and $u^\alpha=\prod_i u_i^{\alpha_i}$, and define $$\Phi_\alpha(z)=\exp(-\|u(z)\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2))\frac{u(z)^\alpha}{\sigma^{|\alpha|}\sqrt{\alpha!}}.$$ Multiplying the convergent exponential power series in the $d$ coordinates yields $$\sum_\alpha\Phi_\alpha(z)\Phi_\alpha(w)=e^{-(\|u(z)\|_2^2+\|u(w)\|_2^2)/(2\sigma^2)}e^{u(z)\cdot u(w)/\sigma^2}=k_\sigma(z,w).$$ The series is absolutely convergent, since replacing each coordinate product by its absolute value gives the finite value $e^{-(\|u(z)\|_2^2+\|u(w)\|_2^2)/(2\sigma^2)}\exp(\sum_i|u_i(z)u_i(w)|/\sigma^2)$. In particular the vector $\Phi(z)=(\Phi_\alpha(z))_\alpha$ is square summable with squared norm $k_\sigma(z,z)=1$.

For any finite set of points $z_1,\ldots,z_q\in\Omega$ and real coefficients $a_1,\ldots,a_q$, the reproducing property gives $$\left\|\sum_{j=1}^qa_jk_\sigma(\cdot,z_j)\right\|_{\mathcal H_\sigma}^2=\sum_{j,l=1}^qa_ja_lk_\sigma(z_j,z_l)=\left\|\sum_{j=1}^qa_j\Phi(z_j)\right\|_{\ell^2}^2.$$ The second equality follows from step 1.1 by interchanging a finite sum with an absolutely convergent series. Thus this norm identity concerns finite kernel combinations and requires no description of the whole Gaussian RKHS or extension of its functions to $\mathbb R^d$. The RKHS used here is available under the stated Countable Choice hypothesis.

Fix $X$ as in the Statement, set $h=h_X$, and for now choose an integer $n\ge1$ such that $2nh/L\le\kappa$. Fix any $x\in\Omega$ and take coefficients $\lambda_j$ from [F4]. Define real coefficients $$b_j=\lambda_j\exp\left(\frac{\|u(x_j)\|_2^2-\|u(x)\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).$$ Then $\sum_j|b_j|\le e^{t/2}A^n$. For every $|\alpha|\le n$, the polynomial $z\mapsto u(z)^\alpha$ has total degree at most $n$, so reproduction implies $$\sum_jb_j\Phi_\alpha(x_j)=\frac{e^{-\|u(x)\|_2^2/(2\sigma^2)}}{\sigma^{|\alpha|}\sqrt{\alpha!}}\sum_j\lambda_ju(x_j)^\alpha=\Phi_\alpha(x).$$ Consequently all coordinates of $\Phi(x)-\sum_jb_j\Phi(x_j)$ with $|\alpha|\le n$ vanish.

Write $\Phi_{>n}(z)$ for the coordinates with $|\alpha|>n$. Expanding $(\sum_i u_i(z)^2/\sigma^2)^r$ by multiplication shows that its monomial coefficient at multi-index $\alpha$ of size $r$ is $r!/\alpha!$: it counts the ordered $r$ choices of coordinates with the prescribed multiplicities. Hence $$\|\Phi_{>n}(z)\|_{\ell^2}^2=e^{-\|u(z)\|_2^2/\sigma^2}\sum_{r=n+1}^{\infty}\frac{(\|u(z)\|_2^2/\sigma^2)^r}{r!}\le\sum_{r=n+1}^{\infty}\frac{t^r}{r!}.$$ If $n+2\ge2t$, the ratio of any successive terms in the last tail is at most $1/2$, so summing the geometric majorant gives $$\sum_{r=n+1}^{\infty}\frac{t^r}{r!}\le\frac{2t^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}\le2\left(\frac{et}{n+1}\right)^{n+1}.$$ For the final inequality, $\log(q!)=\sum_{j=1}^q\log j\ge\int_1^q\log s\,ds=q\log q-q+1$ for every integer $q\ge1$, and exponentiation yields $q!\ge(q/e)^q$. Thus the bound holds uniformly for every $z\in\Omega$.

By [F3], the infimum defining $P_X(x)$ is attained by orthogonal projection onto the finite section span. The vector $\sum_j b_jk_\sigma(\cdot,x_j)$ is in that span, so its error norm is an upper bound for $P_X(x)$. Steps 2.1 and 2.2 show that its error norm is $\|\Phi_{>n}(x)-\sum_jb_j\Phi_{>n}(x_j)\|_{\ell^2}$. Apply the triangle inequality to these finitely many square-summable vectors and use steps 2.2 and 2.3 to obtain $$P_X(x)\le\sqrt2(1+e^{t/2}A^n)\left(\frac{et}{n+1}\right)^{(n+1)/2}.$$ The $\ell^2$ triangle inequality here can be obtained from the finite Euclidean triangle inequality on every initial finite collection of multi-indices and then passing to the supremum of their squared partial sums; thus no additional choice principle is involved. The bound is independent of $x$, and holds whenever $n\ge1$, $2nh/L\le\kappa$, and $n+2\ge2t$.

Put $D=\kappa L/2>0$ and $n=\lfloor D/h\rfloor$. For all sufficiently small $h>0$ this integer satisfies $n\ge1$, $n+2\ge2t$, and $D/(2h)\le n\le D/h$; the lower bound follows from $\lfloor s\rfloor\ge s/2$ for $s\ge2$. Also $2nh/L\le\kappa$. Since $1+e^{t/2}A^n\le2e^{t/2}A^n$, the logarithm of the positive bound in step 3.1 is at most $$-\frac12(n+1)\log(n+1)+K(n+1),$$ where one may take $K=1+\frac32\log2+t/2+\log A+\frac12|\log(et)|>0$. Decrease $h_0>0$ until for all $0<h\le h_0$ the preceding integer conditions hold, $h<1$, $\log(n+1)\ge4K$, and $\log(n+1)\ge\frac12|\log h|$. Such an $h_0$ exists because $n\ge D/(2h)$ implies $\log(n+1)\ge|\log h|+\log(D/2)$, which tends to infinity and eventually exceeds $|\log h|/2$.

For $0<h\le h_0$ the exponent in step 4.1 is at most $-(n+1)\log(n+1)/4$, and hence at most $-D|\log h|/(16h)$, by the two lower bounds for $n$ and $\log(n+1)$. Therefore step 3.1 gives, uniformly in $x\in\Omega$, $$P_X(x)\le\exp\left(-\frac D{16}\frac{|\log h|}{h}\right).$$ Taking the supremum over $x$ proves the Statement with $c=D/16$ and $C=1$, and also with any larger positive $C$. All constants depend only on $d$, $\Omega$, and $\sigma$. Countable Choice was used only through the canonical RKHS supplier in step 2.1; the reproduction and feature estimates add no further choice assumption.
